soil-bio-164.title: The common mycorrhizal network and its disputed powers
soil-bio-164.text: Trees in a forest may be linked underground, though how much passes along the links is disputed. A common mycorrhizal network forms where the hyphae of mycorrhizal fungi join the roots of two or more plants, of the same or different species. Suzanne Simard described these networks in 1997, and their apparent roles in woodland earned them the nickname 'Wood Wide Web'. The two main types follow their fungi: arbuscular hyphae enter root cells, while ectomycorrhizal hyphae thread between them. Studies report carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus moving between plants, with nitrogen flowing from nitrogen-fixing to non-fixing plants. Carbon labelling showed carbon passing both ways between paper birch and Douglas fir, and the fir ended with a 2% to 3% net gain. An insect-damaged Douglas fir appeared to warn a nearby ponderosa pine, which then made defense enzymes. Critics call these claims weakly supported. Connections are hard to verify in the field, and the birch-to-fir carbon was not shown to travel through a network rather than through the soil.

soil-bio-183.title: Glomus, a large genus of root fungi
soil-bio-183.text: With about 85 described species, Glomus is the largest genus of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, and every species in it forms mycorrhizae with plant roots. It is not a natural group, though: its members do not all descend from one shared ancestor. The species are thought to be obligate symbionts that cannot be cultured without a host. They live in nearly all land habitats, from farmland and deserts to tundra. Several, such as G. aggregatum, are cultured and sold as mycorrhizal inoculant for farm soils. Not every member helps: G. macrocarpum causes tobacco stunt disease.

soil-bio-151.title: The root microbiome, the company a root keeps
soil-bio-151.text: Before the 1970s, most scientists thought microbes blanketed the whole root surface. In fact they cover about 10% of three-week-old root segments and about 37% of three-month-old roots. The root microbiome is the changing community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, fungi and archaea, that lives with plant roots. The communities inside the root, in the rhizosphere and in bulk soil differ, though some species overlap. Helpful members include nitrogen-fixing bacteria, growth-promoting microbes, mycorrhizal fungi, protozoa and organisms that fight disease. Some bacteria, fungi and nematodes do harm. Root partners live on carbon-rich products of the host's photosynthesis. Mycorrhizal fungi stretch far into the bulk soil, widening the root system's reach. Archaea that make methane or oxidize ammonia are common, especially in wetlands and other soils without oxygen. Plants also pick their company: in finger millet, only about 8% of the core microbiota was consistently shared between soil and plant.

soil-bio-154.title: Rhizobacteria, the bacteria that live on roots
soil-bio-154.text: Not every bacterium on a root is a friend. Rhizobacteria are bacteria that live with plant roots and can harm plant growth, leave it alone or help it. In practice the word usually means the helpful ones, described in {{ref:soil-bio-155}}; they make up about 2–5% of rhizosphere bacteria. Some colonize the root surface or the spaces between outer root cells, often forming nodules. Others live as endophytes inside the plant, in the apoplast, the spaces outside its cells. One of their most useful acts is turning N2 gas, which plants cannot use, into ammonia the host can take up. That service is costly. Building and keeping nodules can take 12–25% of a plant's total photosynthetic output. Rhizobacteria also release organic acids and phosphatases that turn insoluble soil phosphorus into usable forms such as H2PO4−. Free-living nitrogen fixers live just outside the roots of many grasses. In rice they supply more fixed nitrogen when the plant's demand is high. Organic amendments such as sugarcane straw, goat manure and filter mud boost these free-living helpers, even without nodules.

soil-bio-178.title: Rhizobia, the bacteria that feed legumes nitrogen
soil-bio-178.text: Every year 12–20 million hectares of soybeans are inoculated with live bacteria. Those bacteria are rhizobia: soil bacteria that fix nitrogen once they have settled inside swellings on legume roots, described in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}. Rhizobium leguminosarum, the first known species, was identified in 1889. Rhizobia are a mixed group of alpha- and betaproteobacteria, mostly in the order Hyphomicrobiales. They live freely in the soil but need a plant host to fix nitrogen. Inside the nodule they turn atmospheric N2 into ammonia, which is exported to fuel the legume's growth. In return the plant feeds them organic acids, mainly malate and succinate, as their carbon and energy source. It is a classic mutualism. When the legume dies, its nodules break down and release the bacteria back into the soil. Much fixed nitrogen leaves the field in harvested grain or hay. Enough stays behind, as higher soil nitrate, to feed the next crop, which matters most where no fertilizer is used. Inoculation tends to raise yields, and inoculants have been used in North America for over 100 years. The partnership has its cheats. Some strains hoard plant resources while fixing little nitrogen. Legumes answer by sanctioning poorly fixing nodules, cutting their growth or their supply of carbon or oxygen. Conditions matter too. Nutrient deposition has favored less productive strains, and extra nitrogen lets other plants outcompete legumes for light.

soil-bio-184.title: Rhizophagus irregularis, a fungus sold by the bag
soil-bio-184.text: One fungus turns up in many commercial mycorrhizal fertilizers. Rhizophagus irregularis, formerly called Glomus intraradices, is an arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus used as a soil inoculant in agriculture and horticulture. It occurs in almost all soils, especially in forests and grasslands, and most crops benefit from inoculation with it. Studies show it raises phosphorus uptake in many plants, and its hyphae improve soil aggregation. It colonizes new plants from spores, hyphae or colonized root fragments. Researchers use it widely to study how arbuscular fungi improve plants and soil.

soil-bio-167.title: Sugar for phosphorus: the arbuscular bargain
soil-bio-167.text: Phosphorus can flow into mycorrhizae up to six times faster than into root hairs. That speed explains why so many plants buy their phosphorus from fungi. Arbuscular mycorrhizal nutrient exchange is the trade in which these fungi take sugars from their host and supply it above all with phosphorus. Phosphorus reaches roots mainly by diffusion, a slow creep through soil water, and fungal hyphae shorten the distance. In some cases the hyphal network takes over uptake entirely, and all of a plant's phosphorus comes through the fungus. The fungi take the host's photosynthetic products as hexoses, simple sugars. They store carbon as trehalose, glycogen and lipids, and about 25% of the carbon they receive is stored in their hyphae outside the root. The bargain is reciprocal. More carbon to the fungus means more phosphorus back to the plant, and less means less. Some fungi are poor partners that take much carbon for little phosphorus. The fungi also change the root zone. By taking up ammonium selectively and releasing H+ ions, they lower the pH, which makes phosphorus precipitates more soluble. Their ammonium uptake also raises the flow of nitrogen to the plant. As the hyphal network grows and dies back, it adds a substantial amount of carbon to the rhizosphere and to the organic carbon stored below ground.

soil-bio-168.title: Farming with arbuscular fungi instead of against them
soil-bio-168.text: Plowing a field tears up more than soil. It breaks the soil's larger structure and the fungal hyphal network, leaving the fungus unable to infect new roots and cutting the plant's phosphorus supply. Managing arbuscular mycorrhizae in agriculture means arranging {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, fertilizer and cropping so that crops can keep working partnerships with these fungi. Heavy fertilizer and fungicide use, poor rotations and breeding for such conditions all hinder the partnership. Heavy phosphorus fertilizer inhibits colonization: as plant phosphorus rises, the fungus's carbon drain stops paying. Losing the fungi can then cause shortages of micronutrients such as copper. Systems that till less may need less phosphorus fertilizer. Cover crops extend fungal growth through autumn, winter and spring, and the fungus survives winter to colonize the next crop early. Crops poor at finding nutrients, such as flax, depend heavily on the fungi at low and intermediate soil phosphorus. The payoff is greatest in organic and low-input systems, where soil phosphorus is generally low.

soil-bio-141.title: Root mucilage, the slime that greases every root tip
soil-bio-141.text: Plants use up to 40% of the energy they make by photosynthesis secreting one product: slime. Root mucilage is a gelatinous secretion of plant-specific polysaccharides, long chains of sugars, that coats the root cap as part of the root exudate. How it is secreted is still debated. Growing evidence points to root-cap cells that are continually shed and burst as roots push through soil, releasing polysaccharides made in their Golgi apparatus and cell walls. Maize mucilage is rich in galactose, xylose, arabinose, rhamnose and glucose, the building blocks of pectin and other plant polysaccharides. Mucilage glues soil to the root, keeping the contact needed to regulate water uptake. It cuts friction as roots penetrate and maintains a microclimate. It can also reduce evaporation and store water, which helps plants cope with water deficit. Soil fungi feed on broken-down mucilage and in return raise the plant's uptake of water and nutrients, particularly phosphorus.

soil-bio-176.title: Ericoid mycorrhiza, the heath plants' nitrogen miners
soil-bio-176.text: On bogs and heathlands, mineral nitrogen is very scarce, yet heath plants thrive there. Ericoid mycorrhiza is part of the reason: a mutualism between plants of the heath family, Ericaceae, and several lineages of mycorrhizal fungi. The fungi form coils inside the epidermal cells of fine hair roots. Each coil, where soil nutrients are traded for plant sugars, works for only a few weeks before degrading. Their enzymes break down complex organic molecules, taking nitrogen even from cellulose, pectin, chitin and the woody compound described in {{ref:soil-bio-116}}. In acidic, slowly decaying litter layers they pass that nitrogen straight to their hosts.

soil-bio-192.title: Siderophores, the iron hooks of soil microbes
soil-bio-192.text: Soil is full of iron, yet plants and microbes can still starve for it. In aerobic soils iron is mostly ferric (Fe3+), which forms insoluble, rust-like solids. Siderophores solve the problem. They are small iron-binding compounds secreted by bacteria, fungi and some plants, and they are among the strongest known Fe3+ binders. They pull iron into soluble complexes that cells take up by active transport. Microbes switch on production when iron runs short. Plants on calcareous soils, 30% of the world's farmland, often lack iron; grasses, cereals and rice answer by secreting phytosiderophores such as deoxymugineic acid. Siderophores from rhizosphere microbes raise iron availability to plants, and oats can take up iron through them. Fluorescent pseudomonads make pyoverdine siderophores that starve pathogens of iron. Siderophores can also chelate other metals, from aluminum and copper to lead, cadmium and uranium.

soil-bio-179.title: Root nodules, the pink factories of fixed nitrogen
soil-bio-179.text: Cut open a working nodule and its fixing zone is pink, colored by leghemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that manages oxygen. A root nodule is a growth on the roots of some plants, chiefly legumes, that houses nitrogen-fixing bacteria: rhizobia in legumes, or Frankia in other plants. Fixation is very sensitive to oxygen. Nodules form when soil nitrogen is scarce; plenty of it blocks them. Legume roots release flavonoids that attract rhizobia and switch on nod factors. These make root hairs curl, and an infection thread carries the bacteria into the cortex. Leaf sugars pay for splitting N2. Determinate nodules, as on soybean, stop dividing early and are round. Indeterminate ones, as on pea, alfalfa and clover, keep a growing tip and are cylindrical. Heat, acidic soils, drought and nitrate limit it. When the plant dies, its fixed nitrogen fertilizes the soil, which is why traditional rotations include a legume such as clover.

soil-bio-150.title: The spermosphere, a seed's first neighborhood
soil-bio-150.text: Within hours of planting, a seed can be under attack. Pathogens such as Fusarium and Pythium ultimum may colonize it, though helpful microbes the seed attracts can keep them out. The contest plays out in the spermosphere, the zone around a germinating seed where soil, microbes and seed interact. It typically reaches 1–10 mm from the seed, varying with seed type, soil microbes and moisture. Seed exudates inhibit or stimulate microbes, but the soil's organic matter matters more. Once the radicle emerges, it grows into the rhizosphere below, and above into the zone around the stem described in {{ref:soil-bio-073}} and onto the leaf surfaces.

soil-bio-146.title: Allelopathy, chemical warfare from the roots
soil-bio-146.text: Some plants fight their neighbors with chemistry. Allelopathy is the release by some plants, often from their roots, of chemicals that hold back the growth of other organisms. Invasive garlic mustard is believed to stop trees forming mycorrhizae in North American forests. Its chemical weapon, benzyl isothiocyanate, inhibited three ectomycorrhizal fungi on white pine seedlings. Farmers turn the effect on weeds: cover crops such as rye, hairy vetch, red clover, sorghum-sudangrass and mustards suppress them this way. Rotating crops relieves allelopathy and also raises yields through better nutrient availability.

soil-bio-147.title: Reading the root zone through its genes and chemistry
soil-bio-147.text: Most life around a root is invisible, so researchers read it through genes and chemistry. Rhizosphere research methods range from pH measurements to DNA sequencing of its microbes. Marker genes, 16S rRNA for bacteria and the ITS region for fungi, are amplified and sequenced to reveal a community's makeup and diversity. Metagenomics and metatranscriptomics sequence all the DNA or RNA present, showing what a community could do and which genes are active. Microelectrodes, agar techniques and microsampling follow pH and water movement near roots. Pyrolysis–field ionization mass spectrometry detects the dark organic acids and residues of decayed matter in field soils.

soil-bio-145.title: The chemical conversation around roots
soil-bio-145.text: Roots send chemical messages, and the soil around them is full of listeners. Rhizosphere signalling is the exchange of chemical signals among roots, microbes, fungi and insects, which decides who colonizes the root zone. Hundreds of root metabolites recruit microbes, letting plants favor helpful bacteria. Rhizobia detect flavonoids from legume roots and reply with nod factors that lead to root nodules, and each signal pair is strictly specific. Root signals described in {{ref:soil-bio-172}} make mycorrhizal spores germinate and colonize the root. There are eavesdroppers. The parasitic plant Striga germinates when it detects the same signals.

soil-bio-160.title: Dual mycorrhiza, plants with two kinds of partner
soil-bio-160.text: A few plant species refuse to choose between fungal partners. Dual mycorrhiza is their ability to host both arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal fungi in the same root system at once. Its costs and benefits seem to depend on the plant's life stage and on nonliving conditions, and switching between fungal types has also been reported. Dual-mycorrhizal plants often have broader ranges, spreading into habitats where one fungal type is missing. They aid succession and recovery on nutrient-poor soils and are valued in restoration where trees lack fungal inoculum. Ectomycorrhizal woodland trees have been seen establishing around dual-mycorrhizal willows amid vegetation dominated by arbuscular partnerships.

soil-bio-165.title: From a pale forest plant to a fungal genome
soil-bio-165.text: The study of root-fungus partnerships began with a puzzling plant. In 1881 Franciszek Kamieński showed that Monotropa hypopitys depends on fungi from neighboring trees for nutrition. In 1885 A.B. Frank formally described and named mycorrhizal fungi. In 1899 Noël Bernard established that orchids such as Neottia nidus-avis need a specific fungus to germinate. Paleobotanists working on the Rhynie chert later showed that mycorrhiza-like associations existed in early land plants 407 million years ago. In 2008 Laccaria bicolor became the first ectomycorrhizal fungus to have its genome sequenced, opening the molecular era of the field.

soil-bio-163.title: Mycorrhizae in a warming, polluted world
soil-bio-163.text: Extra carbon dioxide in the air sounds like a gift to plants and their fungi. If nothing else is limiting, more carbon dioxide should directly benefit both. Yet climate change may also damage mycorrhizae. They tend to do better in cool conditions, so warming could harm them. That matters most in the Arctic, where nitrogen and water are hard to get and the fungi are crucial to plant growth. Pollution adds pressure. SO2, NOx and ozone from human activity may reduce fungal propagules, root colonization, links between trees and ectomycorrhizal enzyme activity. The breakdown of excess atmospheric ammonia can damage fine mycorrhizal structures.

soil-bio-162.title: Why plants struggle on barren soil without fungi
soil-bio-162.text: Plant a seedling in sterile soil and it often does poorly, unless someone adds spores or hyphae of mycorrhizal fungi to colonize its roots. Without these fungi, plant growth can lag in early succession and on degraded land. The fungi can also tilt competition. Introducing alien mycorrhizal plants into nutrient-poor ecosystems puts native non-mycorrhizal plants at a disadvantage. Some partnerships bring extra help. Knobbly ectomycorrhizae of Suillus tomentosus on lodgepole pine host nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which let the pines colonize nutrient-poor sites.
